screens.title: File Permissions & Ownership
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll build a clear mental model of Linux file permissions and ownership and then apply that model to secure files and shared directories. We begin by defining the three basic permissions — read, write, execute — and who they apply to: the file owner, the file's group, and everyone else. You will practice both symbolic and octal chmod styles so you can read and set permissions quickly. We'll also cover ownership changes with chown and chgrp, and the special permission bits that change runtime behavior: SUID, SGID, and the sticky bit. Finally, you'll see how Access Control Lists let you grant specific users or groups permissions without changing the base owner/group settings. Understanding these controls is essential for preventing accidental data loss, avoiding privilege escalation, and enabling safe collaboration. For example, a shared project folder can use SGID so files inherit a team group, and setfacl to give a QA user read-only access. By the end you'll be able to audit permission strings, fix common mistakes like forgetting recursive changes, and choose between standard permissions and ACLs when appropriate. Think about one directory you manage now — what minimal changes would reduce accidental writes while preserving team access?

screens.title: The rwx model: what read, write, execute mean
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the three basic permissions and why they differ between files and directories. Read grants the ability to view file contents. For a directory, read allows listing the filenames inside, but it doesn't let you open or change those files. Write permits modifying a file's contents; on directories, write allows creating, renaming, or removing entries within the directory. Execute on a file means the file can be run as a program or script. On a directory, execute is the permission that allows entering the directory and accessing inodes by name; without execute you cannot cd into it or traverse into subdirectories even if you can list names. A concrete example: a configuration file should often be readable by a service account but not writable by general users. Set the file to rw-r----- so the owner and service group can read, but others cannot. A common misconception is treating directory read as equivalent to execute; you may see names but still be unable to open files without execute. Another example: making a script executable (chmod +x) is necessary for running it directly; merely having read and write does not permit execution. Understanding this difference prevents accidental lockouts or overexposure when you set permissions on folders and files. Consider: which permission would you grant to allow a user to create files but not list other users' files?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Read, write, and execute mean different things on files and directories; execute on directories enables traversal.

content.html:
Core Concept
r, w, x — concrete meanings

File — read: view contents; write: change contents; execute: run as a program.

Directory — read: list names; write: create/delete entries; execute: traverse and access entries by name.

Misconception: listing file names (read) is not sufficient to open files without execute on the directory.

Key Takeaway

Treat directory execute as traversal permission; set directory bits intentionally to control access to contents.

Examples & analogy
File: script.sh — chmod 755
Owner: read/write/execute; others: read and execute. Necessary to run the script as a program.
Directory: /data — chmod 750
Owner: full; group: read+execute to view and traverse; others: none. Prevents public access while allowing group collaboration.
Analogy
Think of a directory as a locked hallway. Read shows the door names; execute opens the door to go inside.

screens.title: Reading the permission string (ls -l)
screens.narratorSegment: When you run ls -l you get a 10-character string like -rwsr-sr-- or drwxrwxrwt. Learning to read this string quickly lets you audit permissions without guessing. The first character shows type: dash for a regular file, d for directory. The following nine characters are three triplets: owner, group, others. Each triplet has r, w, x positions; an absent permission is a dash. Special bits replace execute letters with s or t when set: owner's execute position shows s for SUID, group's execute shows s for SGID, and others' execute shows t for the sticky bit on directories. A plus sign after the string indicates ACLs are present. Concrete example: drwxrws--- means a directory where owner has full rights, group has read/write and SGID is set, others have no access; new files inherit the directory group. A typical mistake is failing to notice the leading character and assuming a directory bit applies to a file. Another is missing the trailing + and overlooking ACL rules. Practice: run ls -l on a few system locations like /tmp and /etc to observe sticky, SUID, and SGID in action. Which character tells you that ACLs are present on a file?

keyIdea.title: Decode ls -l
keyIdea.text: First char is type, next nine are three rwx triplets; s and t indicate special bits, + shows ACL presence.

content.html:
Process Flow
Reading the permission string

Type char: - (file) or d (directory). Then owner, group, others triplets: r w x. Special bits replace x with s or t.

Trailing plus indicates an ACL is set.

-rwsr-sr--  1 root root  14768 Jun  1 12:34 passwd
drwxrwxrwt 10 root root  4096 Jun  6 09:02 /tmp
-rw-r--r--+ 1 root root   234 Jun  2 08:00 config.conf
Example outputs: note s for SUID/SGID, t for sticky, and + for ACLs.
Explainer cards
Owner triplet
Controls what the file owner can do. Look here first when troubleshooting access for the file owner.
Group triplet
Group permissions enable team collaboration. SGID in this triplet affects newly created child files in directories.
Others triplet
Least-privilege zone. Keep these bits strict to avoid exposing data to all users.
Quick check: the presence of '+' after the mode means ACLs exist and may override or supplement the basic bits.

screens.title: chmod symbolic mode — targeted tweaks
screens.narratorSegment: Symbolic chmod provides a readable way to adjust permissions for specific entities without recalculating numbers. The pattern is entity-operator-permission, for example u+w adds write to the owner, o-rwx removes all permissions for others, and ug+rw adds read and write for both owner and group. You can combine operations with commas: chmod u+w,g-w,o-r file. txt. Symbolic mode is useful when you need a small change and want the intention to be obvious to another administrator reading your commands. A concrete example: you find a script owned by alice that lacks execute for the owner; run sudo chmod u+x script. sh to allow alice to run it. Another example: to remove execute for others on a directory, use chmod o-x mydir. A common pitfall is forgetting to use -R when intending to change nested files and directories; symbolic chmod without -R changes only the named node. Also be careful when mixing set and additive operations: chmod u=rw,g=r file will overwrite group or owner bits as specified. Practice crafting symbolic expressions until they feel natural; they make maintenance commands self-documenting and reduce surprising permission changes in multi-admin environments.

keyIdea.title: Symbolic chmod
keyIdea.text: Use characters for entities and operators for readable, targeted permission changes; commas chain operations when needed.

content.html:
Definition
Symbolic chmod

Format: [u|g|o|a][+|-|=][r|w|x]. Combine with commas for multiple operations.

Useful for quick human-readable edits and scripts that should be self-describing.

# add execute for owner
sudo chmod u+x script.sh

# remove all permissions for others on a directory
sudo chmod o-rwx /srv/secret

# add read+write for user and group, remove others
sudo chmod ug+rw,o-r file.txt
Explanation cards
Operator types
+ adds, - removes, = sets exact permissions overwriting previous bits.
Common pitfall
Using = unintentionally removes other bits. Audit before running bulk changes.
Pro tip
Use symbolic mode in interactive work and octal in scripts where compactness matters.
Remember to use -R when you want recursive application to a directory tree.

screens.title: chmod octal mode — concise and script-friendly
screens.narratorSegment: Octal chmod is compact and ideal for scripts or when you need to set all three triplets at once. Each permission maps to a value: read 4, write 2, execute 1. Sum them per entity to form three digits. For instance 7 means full rights (4+2+1), 6 means read+write (4+2), and 5 means read+execute (4+1). Example: chmod 755 sets owner to 7, group to 5, others to 5 — commonly used for executable scripts where everyone may run but only the owner edits. chmod 644 is used for documents: owner read/write, group read, others read. Special bits are represented by a leading digit: 4 for SUID, 2 for SGID, and 1 for sticky; combine them as needed — 2755 sets SGID with standard 755. A common error is miscalculating the sum or forgetting the special leading digit when setting SUID/SGID/sticky. For directory trees use sudo chmod -R 2770 /project/data to set SGID and desired triplets for owner and group. Octal mode reduces human-readable clarity but reduces typing and is less error-prone in scripts when the intended exact mode must be reproduced. Practice translating examples until you can compute digits mentally.

keyIdea.title: Octal chmod
keyIdea.text: Use numeric sums for each triplet; a leading octal digit configures special bits like SUID, SGID, and sticky.

content.html:
Comparison
Octal vs Symbolic
  • Octal is concise and reproducible in scripts.
  • Symbolic is readable and safer for small interactive tweaks.
  • Use a leading octal for SUID/SGID/sticky bits.
# common examples
sudo chmod 755 script.sh   # rwxr-xr-x
sudo chmod 644 document.txt # rw-r--r--

# set SGID on a dir and allow owner/group full access
sudo chmod 2770 /project/data  # rwsrwx--- (2 for SGID)
Quick mental map
Values
4=read, 2=write, 1=execute. Sum per entity.
Leading digit
4=SUID, 2=SGID, 1=sticky. e.g., 4755 sets SUID.
Pro tip
When scripting, prefer octal for repeatable environments; document the meaning in comments.

screens.title: Ownership: chown and chgrp
screens.narratorSegment: Ownership identifies who is responsible for a file and which group it belongs to. The chown command changes the user owner, and optionally the group with the user:group syntax — chown alice:developers file. txt. The chgrp command is a more focused tool to change only the group owner. Important rules: only root can change a file's user owner to someone else; ordinary users can change a file's group only if they are members of the target group and system policy allows it. Use the -R flag for recursive changes when you want to walk a tree. Practical example: to prepare a team folder for collaboration, run sudo chown root:developers /project/data to set the group, then chmod 2770 to enable SGID so new files inherit the developers group. A common mistake is forgetting to set the group on the parent directory before enabling SGID, which prevents inheritance from matching team expectations. Ownership matters for accountability and access: sensitive configs should be owned by root to avoid accidental modification, while shared data should be owned by a service or team group. When planning ownership changes, ask who will manage the files and whether the change requires root privileges.

keyIdea.title: Ownership rules
keyIdea.text: Use chown to change user and group together, chgrp to change group only; root is required to change user ownership to another user.

content.html:
Core Concept
chown and chgrp

chown user[:group] file — change the file owner and optionally the group.

chgrp group file — change only the group ownership.

Only root can change a file's user owner to a different user; group changes may be restricted to group members.

# set directory to root:developers
sudo chown root:developers /project/data

# change only group
sudo chgrp developers somefile.txt

# recursive change
sudo chown -R alice:developers /srv/project
Cards
When to use chown
Assign a new owner when responsibility for files changes, for example service accounts owning their config files.
When to use chgrp
Switch group ownership to enable team access without changing the file owner.
Pitfall
Changing ownership broadly can break service expectations; always verify with ls -l.

screens.title: Special permissions: SUID, SGID, Sticky bit
screens.narratorSegment: Special permissions change how executables run and how directories behave. SUID causes an executable to run with the privileges of the file owner; a classic safe example is the password program, which needs elevated access to update system authentication stores. When SUID is set, the owner's execute position shows an s. SGID on an executable runs with the group owner privileges. More commonly, SGID on a directory enforces that new files created inside inherit the parent directory's group—very useful for team collaboration. The sticky bit applies to directories and prevents users from deleting or renaming files they don't own inside that directory; /tmp uses this behavior so any user may create files but cannot remove others' files. To set these bits with chmod you can use symbolic u+s, g+s, or +t, or the leading octal digit: 4 for SUID, 2 for SGID, 1 for sticky. Security note: SUID and SGID on writable or world-accessible executables can lead to privilege escalation. Audit files with these bits set and remove them if unnecessary. A common misconception is that SUID makes a user root; it only grants the file's owner privileges for that executable, and careful code review of SUID programs is required. Ask yourself which programs genuinely need these elevated behaviors before applying them.

keyIdea.title: Special bits summary
keyIdea.text: SUID/SGID alter runtime privileges; sticky prevents deletion of others' files. Use sparingly and audit regularly.

content.html:
Core Concept
SUID, SGID, sticky — behavior and use

SUID (4): executable runs with owner privileges. Example: passwd needs elevated access to update secure files.

SGID (2): executable runs with group privileges; directory SGID makes new files inherit parent group.

Sticky bit (1): on directories prevents users from deleting files they do not own.

# set SUID on a script (use with caution)
sudo chmod 4755 /usr/local/bin/dummy

# set SGID on shared dir so children inherit group
sudo chmod 2770 /project/data

# set sticky bit on uploads
sudo chmod 1777 /shared_uploads
Security notes
Risk
SUID/SGID programs can be exploited; avoid setting them on writable files or unknown binaries.
Audit
Regularly run find commands to list SUID/SGID files and review whether they are required.
Checklist
When adding special bits, confirm purpose, review code ownership, and test least-privilege behavior.

screens.title: Access Control Lists (ACLs)
screens.narratorSegment: ACLs extend the basic owner/group/others model by allowing you to give a specific user or group distinct permissions on a file or directory. Use setfacl to add or modify entries and getfacl to inspect them. For example, setfacl -m u:john:rw file. txt grants john read and write even if he is not the file owner or in the file's group. When an ACL exists, ls -l shows a plus sign after the mode, indicating extra rules. ACLs are powerful for one-off exceptions, but they can complicate permission management if overused; prefer standard permissions unless you need per-user exceptions. Practical use case: give QA read-only access to a project directory while keeping write privileges for developers. Example commands: sudo setfacl -R -m u:qa1:rx /project/data to recursively grant qa1 read and execute on directories and files; verify with getfacl /project/data. content.html:
Definition
Access Control Lists
ACLs let you specify permissions for particular users or groups without changing the file owner or primary group. They are additive and are indicated by a + in ls -l output.
Commands & example
# grant qa1 read and execute recursively
sudo setfacl -R -m u:qa1:rx /project/data

# allow developers group full access
sudo setfacl -R -m g:developers:rwx /project/data

# view ACLs
getfacl /project/data
Tip: Use -R with care. Overuse of ACLs across many files increases administrative overhead; prefer group ownership when possible.

screens.title: Hands-on: securing /project/data (lab walkthrough)
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough secures /project/data for a developers team and a QA user. We'll follow four steps with commands and verification. Step one: create the directory and set ownership. Running sudo mkdir -p /project/data then sudo chown root:developers /project/data makes root the owner and developers the group. This sets clear responsibility and a team group for collaboration. Step two: apply SGID and restrictive bits with sudo chmod 2770 /project/data. The leading 2 sets SGID so new files inherit the developers group; 770 gives owner and group full access and prevents others. Step three: grant QA read and execute using ACLs so QA can view files but not modify them — sudo setfacl -R -m u:qa1:rx /project/data. Recursive ACL application ensures existing and new files receive the rule. Step four: verify with ls -ld /project/data and getfacl /project/data to confirm mode shows the SGID bit and ACL entries. Common mistakes include forgetting -R, which leaves nested items unchanged, or applying SGID before fixing group ownership. Security implication: SGID simplifies group collaboration but do not set SUID on group-writable executables. After completing these steps, ask whether any service accounts also need access and, if so, add them to the developers group rather than widening others.

content.html:
Live Terminal Demo
Step-by-step commands
# 1. create and set ownership
sudo mkdir -p /project/data
sudo chown root:developers /project/data

# 2. set SGID and permissions (owner root, group developers)
sudo chmod 2770 /project/data

# 3. grant QA read+execute recursively
sudo setfacl -R -m u:qa1:rx /project/data

# 4. verify
ls -ld /project/data
getfacl /project/data
Expected verification
ls -ld should show drwxrws--- and an s in the group execute position, indicating SGID.
getfacl should list an entry for u:qa1:rx confirming QA access.
Check common mistake: if nested files lack correct group, rerun chown -R before setting SGID or ACLs.
Reflect: did you reduce other access while preserving developer workflow? If not, adjust group membership rather than resorting to permissive others bits.

screens.narratorSegment: Summarize the essentials so you remember what to apply in real systems. First, always follow least privilege: set the minimum permissions necessary and prefer group ownership and SGID for team collaboration rather than opening access to others. Second, use the right tool: symbolic chmod for readable, targeted edits, octal chmod for concise scripting, chown/chgrp to assign responsibility, and ACLs only when per-user exceptions are needed. Third, treat special bits with caution: SUID and SGID affect runtime privileges, and the sticky bit protects shared directories; audit any SUID/SGID binaries for security risks. These three rules will guide most decisions when you harden files, prepare a shared workspace, or debug permission problems. A quick verification habit — ls -l plus getfacl when you see a plus sign — ensures changes had the intended effect. Keep this chapter's checklist nearby when you administer RHEL systems.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll build a clear mental model of Linux file permissions and ownership and then apply that model to secure files and shared directories. We begin by defining the three basic permissions — read, write, execute — and who they apply to: the file owner, the file's group, and everyone else. You will practice both symbolic and octal chmod styles so you can read and set permissions quickly. We'll also cover ownership changes with chown and chgrp, and the special permission bits that change runtime behavior: SUID, SGID, and the sticky bit. Finally, you'll see how Access Control Lists let you grant specific users or groups permissions without changing the base owner/group settings. Understanding these controls is essential for preventing accidental data loss, avoiding privilege escalation, and enabling safe collaboration. For example, a shared project folder can use SGID so files inherit a team group, and setfacl to give a QA user read-only access. By the end you'll be able to audit permission strings, fix common mistakes like forgetting recursive changes, and choose between standard permissions and ACLs when appropriate. Think about one directory you manage now — what minimal changes would reduce accidental writes while preserving team access?

These objectives focus on practical competence. First, you will be able to explain read, write, and execute in the context of files and directories and identify owner, group, and others. That matters because permissions are the first line of defense against unauthorized changes. Second, you will learn to apply and change permissions with chmod using both symbolic and octal modes; being fluent in both formats speeds troubleshooting and automation. Third, you'll change file and directory ownership with chown and chgrp. Ownership assigns responsibility and enables group-based collaboration. Fourth, you'll work with special permissions and Access Control Lists so you can implement secure shared directories without granting overly broad access. Each objective pairs a command-level skill with a security rationale and a short mnemonic to help you remember when to use each tool. Together, these skills let you harden sensitive files, set up team directories, and safely manage service binaries that require elevated privileges. As you practice, consider one real file or folder you manage and how each objective would change your handling of it.

This second objectives slide outlines how you'll practice and verify mastery. You'll run ls -l to inspect permission strings and map each character to a capability, then use chmod in symbolic mode for quick adjustments and octal mode when scripting. We'll demonstrate chown and chgrp with examples showing when root is required. Special bits will be applied to sample files and directories to observe behaviour: SUID on an executable to run with file owner privileges, SGID on a group directory so new files inherit the group, and the sticky bit to prevent deletion by others. Finally, the hands-on lab secures a shared project folder using chown, chmod with SGID, and setfacl to grant a QA user read-execute rights. Each practice step includes verification commands — ls -l and getfacl — so you can confirm outcomes. Throughout, I'll point out common mistakes like forgetting -R for recursive changes and the security risk of unnecessary SUID bits. This practice plan ensures you can reproduce and explain each change in a real environment.

Let's define the three basic permissions and why they differ between files and directories. Read grants the ability to view file contents. For a directory, read allows listing the filenames inside, but it doesn't let you open or change those files. Write permits modifying a file's contents; on directories, write allows creating, renaming, or removing entries within the directory. Execute on a file means the file can be run as a program or script. On a directory, execute is the permission that allows entering the directory and accessing inodes by name; without execute you cannot cd into it or traverse into subdirectories even if you can list names. A concrete example: a configuration file should often be readable by a service account but not writable by general users. Set the file to rw-r----- so the owner and service group can read, but others cannot. A common misconception is treating directory read as equivalent to execute; you may see names but still be unable to open files without execute. Another example: making a script executable (chmod +x) is necessary for running it directly; merely having read and write does not permit execution. Understanding this difference prevents accidental lockouts or overexposure when you set permissions on folders and files. Consider: which permission would you grant to allow a user to create files but not list other users' files?

When you run ls -l you get a 10-character string like -rwsr-sr-- or drwxrwxrwt. Learning to read this string quickly lets you audit permissions without guessing. The first character shows type: dash for a regular file, d for directory. The following nine characters are three triplets: owner, group, others. Each triplet has r, w, x positions; an absent permission is a dash. Special bits replace execute letters with s or t when set: owner's execute position shows s for SUID, group's execute shows s for SGID, and others' execute shows t for the sticky bit on directories. A plus sign after the string indicates ACLs are present. Concrete example: drwxrws--- means a directory where owner has full rights, group has read/write and SGID is set, others have no access; new files inherit the directory group. A typical mistake is failing to notice the leading character and assuming a directory bit applies to a file. Another is missing the trailing + and overlooking ACL rules. Practice: run ls -l on a few system locations like /tmp and /etc to observe sticky, SUID, and SGID in action. Which character tells you that ACLs are present on a file?

Symbolic chmod provides a readable way to adjust permissions for specific entities without recalculating numbers. The pattern is entity-operator-permission, for example u+w adds write to the owner, o-rwx removes all permissions for others, and ug+rw adds read and write for both owner and group. You can combine operations with commas: chmod u+w,g-w,o-r file. txt. Symbolic mode is useful when you need a small change and want the intention to be obvious to another administrator reading your commands. A concrete example: you find a script owned by alice that lacks execute for the owner; run sudo chmod u+x script. sh to allow alice to run it. Another example: to remove execute for others on a directory, use chmod o-x mydir. A common pitfall is forgetting to use -R when intending to change nested files and directories; symbolic chmod without -R changes only the named node. Also be careful when mixing set and additive operations: chmod u=rw,g=r file will overwrite group or owner bits as specified. Practice crafting symbolic expressions until they feel natural; they make maintenance commands self-documenting and reduce surprising permission changes in multi-admin environments.

Octal chmod is compact and ideal for scripts or when you need to set all three triplets at once. Each permission maps to a value: read 4, write 2, execute 1. Sum them per entity to form three digits. For instance 7 means full rights (4+2+1), 6 means read+write (4+2), and 5 means read+execute (4+1). Example: chmod 755 sets owner to 7, group to 5, others to 5 — commonly used for executable scripts where everyone may run but only the owner edits. chmod 644 is used for documents: owner read/write, group read, others read. Special bits are represented by a leading digit: 4 for SUID, 2 for SGID, and 1 for sticky; combine them as needed — 2755 sets SGID with standard 755. A common error is miscalculating the sum or forgetting the special leading digit when setting SUID/SGID/sticky. For directory trees use sudo chmod -R 2770 /project/data to set SGID and desired triplets for owner and group. Octal mode reduces human-readable clarity but reduces typing and is less error-prone in scripts when the intended exact mode must be reproduced. Practice translating examples until you can compute digits mentally.

Ownership identifies who is responsible for a file and which group it belongs to. The chown command changes the user owner, and optionally the group with the user:group syntax — chown alice:developers file. txt. The chgrp command is a more focused tool to change only the group owner. Important rules: only root can change a file's user owner to someone else; ordinary users can change a file's group only if they are members of the target group and system policy allows it. Use the -R flag for recursive changes when you want to walk a tree. Practical example: to prepare a team folder for collaboration, run sudo chown root:developers /project/data to set the group, then chmod 2770 to enable SGID so new files inherit the developers group. A common mistake is forgetting to set the group on the parent directory before enabling SGID, which prevents inheritance from matching team expectations. Ownership matters for accountability and access: sensitive configs should be owned by root to avoid accidental modification, while shared data should be owned by a service or team group. When planning ownership changes, ask who will manage the files and whether the change requires root privileges.

Special permissions change how executables run and how directories behave. SUID causes an executable to run with the privileges of the file owner; a classic safe example is the password program, which needs elevated access to update system authentication stores. When SUID is set, the owner's execute position shows an s. SGID on an executable runs with the group owner privileges. More commonly, SGID on a directory enforces that new files created inside inherit the parent directory's group—very useful for team collaboration. The sticky bit applies to directories and prevents users from deleting or renaming files they don't own inside that directory; /tmp uses this behavior so any user may create files but cannot remove others' files. To set these bits with chmod you can use symbolic u+s, g+s, or +t, or the leading octal digit: 4 for SUID, 2 for SGID, 1 for sticky. Security note: SUID and SGID on writable or world-accessible executables can lead to privilege escalation. Audit files with these bits set and remove them if unnecessary. A common misconception is that SUID makes a user root; it only grants the file's owner privileges for that executable, and careful code review of SUID programs is required. Ask yourself which programs genuinely need these elevated behaviors before applying them.
